Moving Through the Broken World

The world of Bad Eden is divided into hexes, fragments of reality left behind after the collapse of Adam Kadmon.

Travel is the process of moving between these fragments.

As your faction explores the world, travel allows you to:

• discover new regions
• reach important locations
• respond to threats
• expand your territory

But movement through the world is never entirely predictable.

Every journey carries risk, discovery, and possibility.

How Travel Works

Travel usually occurs when your faction moves from one hex to another on the campaign map.

The distance traveled and the terrain between locations determine how difficult the journey will be.

During travel, the game may generate:

• encounters
• hazards
• discoveries
• narrative events

These moments help make the world feel alive and responsive to player movement.

Travel Encounters

Travel often triggers encounters, which represent unexpected situations that arise along the journey.

Encounters might include:

• hostile creatures
• strange phenomena
• hidden ruins
• travelers in need
• environmental hazards

These encounters are usually presented through Campaign Beats, where players must make decisions that shape the outcome.

Terrain and Difficulty

Not all regions of the world are equally easy to cross.

Some terrain may slow travel or increase the risk of encounters.

Examples include:

• dense wilderness
• ruined infrastructure
• corrupted environments
• unstable magical fields

Travel through these areas may require more time, resources, or careful planning.

Travel Routes

As your faction expands its territory, travel becomes easier between regions you control.

Developed hexes and infrastructure can create reliable routes that allow faster movement across the map.

This makes territory development strategically important, since safe routes improve mobility and coordination.

Ley Gates

Some locations contain ancient structures known as Ley Gates.

These gates connect distant hexes through currents of magical energy called leylines.

When activated, a Ley Gate allows factions to travel between two distant regions far more quickly than normal travel.

Ley Gates are rare and often require discovery, repair, or control before they can be used.

Travel Hazards

Traveling through the fractured world is not always safe.

Possible dangers include:

• environmental corruption
• radiation zones
• magical anomalies
• hostile factions
• wandering creatures

Hazards may drain resources, create narrative complications, or trigger conflicts.

Planning Expeditions

As your faction grows, travel becomes a strategic decision.

You may need to decide:

• which regions to explore next
• when to respond to threats
• how to connect distant territory
• whether to risk dangerous routes

Exploration is often the first step toward discovering new opportunities and new problems to solve.

The Journey Cycle

Travel often follows a simple pattern:

Choose Destination
      ↓
Begin Journey
      ↓
Encounter Events
      ↓
Resolve Problems
      ↓
Arrive in New Hex

Once you arrive, exploration of the new hex can begin.

Travel and Exploration

Travel is the gateway to discovery.

Every new region you enter may reveal:

• hidden settlements
• forgotten infrastructure
• powerful artifacts
• sources of corruption
• opportunities for development

The farther your faction travels, the more of the world becomes known — and the more influence you can wield within it.

What Players Should Remember

Three key ideas define travel in Bad Eden.

1 — Travel reveals the world

New hexes mean new stories.

2 — Travel creates risk

Journeys often lead to encounters and challenges.

3 — Travel expands opportunity

Exploration opens the door to growth, resources, and influence.

In Simple Terms

Travel is how your faction moves through the shattered world.

It leads to discovery, danger, and new possibilities.

Every journey pushes the campaign forward.
